name: Artificial intelligence
snapshot: I see more AI use, but value depends on who turns that use into cash. I am interested in bottlenecks in chips, manufacturing and software. Capital is already leaving traces in fund disclosures; the risk is paying today for profits that still have to arrive.
change: I see companies delegating analysis, content and programming tasks to models. The question I care about is how much time or money they save after paying for computing, integration and supervision. That is where the economic story begins.
arguments: In favor, I see documented adoption and computing needs that translate into suppliers’ sales. If customers sustain those savings, there is a basis for recurring demand.
Against it, I see an infrastructure bill arriving before some of the benefits. Competition can pass savings through to customers and leave suppliers with less margin.
invalidation: If customer savings and incremental revenue persistently fail to cover computing and integration, I would revisit the business thesis. If the business works but the price requires extraordinary results, I would revisit the vehicle and its valuation.
value: I would start where switching suppliers really costs something: EUV lithography, advanced manufacturing and software ecosystems. Then I would work through margins, reinvestment and the price paid. An excellent company can still be a weak investment if I buy it as though nothing could go wrong.
evidence_text: For Europe I have the Eurostat series. In the United States, Census finds 18% of businesses using AI in its reference period; employment-weighted, the figure is 32%. I would show them separately: their questions, periods and populations do not justify a Europe-versus-US race with two bars stripped of context.

risks.title: Investing faster than cash arrives
risks.mechanism: A data center is paid for before its full utilization is known. If revenue and savings take time, spending can consume cash even while sales grow.
risks.evidence: Microsoft reports USD 58,000 million of operating cash flow and USD 39,367 million of equipment payments from July to September 2026. The difference is USD 18,633 million, versus USD 25,663 million a year earlier; this is my consolidated calculation, not AI-only cash flow.
risks.watch: If investment keeps growing faster than operating cash flow, I would review utilization, purchase commitments and capital recovery.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

risks.title: A bottleneck also concentrates fragility
risks.mechanism: Export licenses, manufacturing capacity or a sole supplier can slow deliveries and raise component costs. A commercial advantage does not remove that dependency.
risks.evidence: ASML identifies Carl Zeiss SMT as the sole supplier of critical optics. NVIDIA describes export restrictions, competition and dependence on third parties in its 10-Q.
risks.watch: If licenses tighten or lead times rise, I would review deliverable orders, inventories and customers’ real alternatives.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

risks.title: The model works but the product does not pay off
risks.mechanism: Errors, sensitive data and supervision can consume the promised savings. Competitors or major customers’ own chips can also reduce the price a supplier charges.
risks.evidence: NIST documents risks specific to generative AI; NVIDIA acknowledges competition and technological change. These are identified mechanisms, not a numerical probability of failure.
risks.watch: If customers do not renew or cost per task does not fall, I would review net savings, margins and the ability to replace the supplier.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

name: Automation
snapshot: I see more industrial tasks being automated and demand that varies by country. I would look for suppliers embedded in the factory, with maintenance and demonstrable savings. Fund positions are a clue about capital, not a guarantee. The cycle and rules differ between the US and Europe; I focus on whether installation costs more than it saves.
change: Automation interests me when it reduces errors, downtime or cost per unit. Sensors, control and software become part of the factory’s daily process. For the customer, the calculation includes installation, maintenance and staff training.
arguments: I see demand when workers are scarce, errors are expensive or quality needs to be consistent. The installed base can sustain service and spare parts.
I also see a business tied to the industrial cycle. If a plant has spare capacity, it can postpone a technically sound improvement.
invalidation: If actual savings stay below total installation and operating costs over several relevant cycles, I would revisit the supplier thesis. One weak quarter of orders, on its own, tells me less.
value: I would look at the installed base, the cost of replacing the control system and the service that keeps a factory running. That integration can provide an advantage; then I would check whether it translates into margins and cash, and how much I am paying for it.
evidence_text: I read robot installations as physical adoption. I would separate new units, the installed stock and forecasts, then compare regions within the same IFR statistics.

name: Energy and infrastructure
snapshot: Electricity demand needs generation, grids and connections. I see potential value in equipment that is difficult to replace and assets with regulated revenue. Investment and disclosed positions identify specific actors, with limits. The US and Europe have different permits and tariffs; if returns do not cover debt and construction, the need for energy does not save the investment.
change: I see more electricity demand and projects needing to connect. The bottleneck can be a substation, a transformer or a permit, even when generation capacity exists. That is why I follow the whole chain before choosing a technology.
arguments: Grid renewal and the need for reliable supply can sustain demand for years.
Permits, financing and regulation can delay revenue or pass much of the benefit on to users.
invalidation: If projects do not reach operation, utilization disappoints or the permitted tariff fails to cover the cost of capital, I would revisit the thesis. More announced investment would not be enough for me.
value: I would look at equipment with difficult certification, recurring service and grids with territorial exclusivity. In a regulated monopoly, the question is what return the regulator allows. Having few rivals does not provide freedom to charge any price.
evidence_text: I separate estimated investment, queued projects and operating assets. A connection request shows me intent; it does not yet establish generation, energy sales or returns.

name: Health and longevity
snapshot: I see an aging population and a growing need for diagnosis, treatment and care. I would look for demonstrated clinical benefits, reimbursable revenue and real barriers to copying the product. Funds show increases and reductions, not consensus. In the US and Europe, the payer changes the economics; patents, prices and litigation can reduce value even as demand grows.
change: I am interested in how care changes with age: prevention, diagnosis, treatment and ongoing care. Aging describes a need. To turn that into a business, someone must demonstrate outcomes and someone must pay for them.
arguments: Age and chronic illness can sustain recurring use of useful services and devices.
A product can work clinically yet receive an insufficient price. A trial can also fail, or patent protection can expire.
invalidation: If a treatment does not provide a meaningful clinical improvement or the payer does not accept its cost, I would revisit the product thesis. If a patent expires, I would separately review how much business the company can defend.
value: I would look at devices with associated training and consumables, diagnostics with proven usefulness and treatments protected by active patents. A barrier has an expiry date, substitutes and pricing rules; I would run those numbers before calling it a durable advantage.
evidence_text: Demographics help me understand the need. To value a business, I would connect them with clinical outcomes, spending and reimbursement, preserving the distinction between observations and projections.

name: Cybersecurity
snapshot: I see AI making some scams cheaper, with businesses and people more exposed. Complaints and surveys measure part of the problem; they do not predict how much of the population will become victims. I would examine identity, fraud prevention and response. Capital and rules help locate demand; I focus on whether more attacks translate into margins for any given supplier.
change: AI makes fabricated messages, voices and documents more convincing. I am interested in how that combines with fast payments and criminal networks operating across countries. For a business, damage can arrive through a system or a deceived person.
arguments: I see a persistent need to authenticate identities, protect systems and respond to incidents.
Customers may consolidate purchases into fewer platforms. A greater need for security does not ensure growth for every vendor.
invalidation: If renewals and retention fall while the cost of protecting customers rises, I would revisit the supplier thesis. I would also revisit it if its products fail to reduce the risk they promise to control.
value: I would look at who is integrated into identity, access and operations, and how much replacing them costs the customer. Integration and data can give a platform an advantage; that same concentration requires it to avoid becoming a single point of failure.
evidence_text: I would show 22,364 complaints mentioning AI and USD 893.3 million in IC3-adjusted losses in 2025. These are received reports, not unique people. Gallup separately estimates the share of adults who experienced a scam; it does not attribute all those scams to AI.

name: Defense and security
snapshot: I see more demand for defense, but I follow the path from budget to delivery. I would look for certified suppliers, scarce capacity and recurring maintenance. Public procurement and disclosed positions identify real capital. The US and Europe shape contracts and exports; I focus on whether delays and costs consume margins despite a large backlog.
change: Defense needs ammunition, sensors, communications, aircraft and autonomous systems. I look at how much spending becomes executable contracts and which company can deliver without losing money.
arguments: Long programs and maintenance can give hard-to-replace suppliers visibility on demand.
A public buyer can change priorities. A fixed-price contract can become a burden if production costs much more than expected.
invalidation: If awards do not arrive or deliveries persistently consume cash, I would revisit the thesis. An approved budget does not solve that problem for me.
value: I would look at certifications, production capacity and spare parts tied to installed platforms. Sometimes there is only one authorized supplier, but also a buyer with substantial bargaining power. The margin depends on that specific contract.
evidence_text: I read military spending as aggregate public demand. To connect that story to a company, I would examine contracts, timelines, margins and cash collection.

geography.text: I include GAO’s 2026 assessment: major programs continue to show delays, and the average time to deliver capability exceeded 12 years in the portfolio assessed.
I include SAFE: up to EUR 150,000 million in loans for investment and joint procurement. The instrument’s ceiling does not equal awarded contracts or executed spending.

policy.text: I would separate budgets, awards and deliveries. GAO and issuers show delays and cost risks; a strategic priority does not remove the buyer’s bargaining power.
SAFE allows up to EUR 150,000 million in loans. I would distinguish that capacity from the contracts and disbursements actually reaching each manufacturer.

chain.note: I would show economic and operational relationships. Arrow widths are not proportional to money; there are no amounts that would justify presenting these as measured flows.

risks.title: The contract grows while the margin breaks
risks.mechanism: I translate delays and fixed prices into costs that the contractor may have to absorb.
risks.evidence: Lockheed reported unfavorable adjustments in 2026 due to production and delays in F-16s, C-130s and helicopters; GAO documents portfolio delays.
risks.watch: If backlog rises while margins fall, I would review contract type, loss provisions and cash conversion.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

risks.title: The main customer changes priorities
risks.mechanism: I see customer concentration when a budget depends on a few governments.
risks.evidence: Lockheed identifies budget uncertainty, continuing resolutions and government shutdowns; SAFE imposes eligibility and procurement conditions.
risks.watch: Following political announcements, I would review authorizations, actual appropriations and signed contracts before treating them as firm demand.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

risks.title: Technology arrives late
risks.mechanism: I could pay today for a capability that needs more testing and more capital than expected.
risks.evidence: GAO found programs that began rapid acquisition pathways with immature technologies.
risks.watch: If milestones are postponed, I would review technological maturity, customer acceptance and redesign risk; I would not assign the same value to a prototype as to a delivery.
risks.interpretation: The economic mechanism and my monitoring trigger are my interpretation; the source supports the cited evidence.

moat_reading: I would look for certifications, intellectual property, productive capacity and maintenance of installed platforms. Contracts can create lasting relationships, but the government retains bargaining power. I would not call an entire company a monopoly because it is the prime supplier on one program.
